topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A client sends a request, waits one second, and receives a timeout. The natural question is whether to try again. The dangerous assumption is that timeout means nothing happened. The server may have committed the operation and lost the response, or it may still be running after the caller stopped waiting.

topics.title: 8.1.1 Separating Transport Success from Application Success
topics.summary: Transport success means the communication mechanism completed a particular exchange under its rules. Application success means the domain operation established its promised state. These can diverge. A valid response may contain a domain conflict; a broken connection may follow a successful database commit.

topics.title: 8.1.2 Selecting Unary, Streaming, and Asynchronous Operations
topics.summary: A unary request/response operation is appropriate when one bounded request produces one bounded result. A streaming operation can carry multiple messages over one call, but it adds flow control, ordering, cancellation, and long-lived resource ownership. Streaming is not automatically faster or more reliable for every workload.

topics.title: 8.2.1 Using Absolute Local Deadlines
topics.summary: A timeout is a duration; a deadline is a point beyond which the caller is no longer willing to wait. Within one process, convert a duration into an absolute deadline using a monotonic clock and compute remaining time before each phase. This keeps connection establishment, queue residence, transfer, and processing within one caller budget rather than giving each phase a fresh full allowance.

blocks.text: A parent should reserve time for its own completion work. If the full remaining budget is assigned to a child, the child can consume all of it and leave no time for response encoding or delivery. The exact reservation is workload-dependent, but the principle is visible in a simple equation: child allowance is at most parent remaining time minus the parent’s necessary completion margin.

blocks.text: Fan-out makes budgeting more complex. Parallel required children can share a parent deadline, while sequential children consume it one after another. Retrying every child independently can multiply load and make the parent miss its budget even when each local retry policy appears reasonable. Name the layer that owns the retry decision.

topics.title: 8.3.1 Treating Cancellation as a Cooperative Signal
topics.summary: Cancellation communicates that a caller or upstream operation no longer wants ongoing work. It should propagate where doing so saves resources safely. A long computation can periodically check a stop condition; a queued request can be removed before execution; a transport can cancel a pending wait under its API’s rules.

reading.title: 8.3.1 Treating Cancellation as a Cooperative Signal
paragraphs: Cancellation communicates that a caller or upstream operation no longer wants ongoing work. It should propagate where doing so saves resources safely. A long computation can periodically check a stop condition; a queued request can be removed before execution; a transport can cancel a pending wait under its API’s rules.

A handler that is already committing durable state cannot assume cancellation makes the transaction disappear. The application must choose whether to finish the commit, roll back if still possible, or record a compensating action later. That choice depends on the state transition, not only on the RPC status.

The gRPC cancellation documentation emphasizes coordination between the framework and the application handler. It does not generally interrupt arbitrary application code. A service therefore needs explicit cancellation checks and child-operation ownership where those are required. (R11)

Cancellation can also race with normal completion. A robust operation object settles once according to its synchronization rules and still releases resources correctly. A caller should not destroy a borrowed output buffer until completion establishes that no further access is possible, even if it requested cancellation earlier.

topics.title: Failure clinic — Three Layers of Retries
topics.summary: A caller retries a gateway request three times. The gateway retries a worker call three times. The worker retries a database operation three times. Under an outage, one logical request can create up to 27 attempts at the deepest layer, before accounting for any proxy retries. That multiplicative behavior is derived from the chosen counts, not a universal property of retry libraries.
